title: Born in a grove
hookLine: on the road to her parents' home, Maya gives birth holding a branch in the Lumbini garden
last: WHITE ELEPHANT — SOME THINGS ANNOUNCE THEMSELVES.

cards: Queen Maya is heavily pregnant, and she wants to go home. Not to the palace: to her parents' home in a town called Devadaha, the way many women of her time went back to their mothers to give birth.
The king has the road smoothed and decorated, and she sets out in a golden palanquin with a crowd of attendants.

Halfway there, the road passes a grove of sal trees in full bloom: flowers everywhere, bees humming, birds singing. She asks to stop and walk in the garden a while. She never makes it to her mother's house.

teach.h: THE BRANCH BENDS TO HER HAND.
teach.b: The grove is called Lumbini. As the story is told, the queen walks to a great sal tree and reaches up, and the branch bends down to her hand. Standing there, holding it, she gives birth.
No palace, no bed, no midwives from court.

The wonders are older still, from the early discourses: the child is received first by gods, two streams of water fall from the sky to wash mother and son, and the baby stands, takes seven steps, looks in every direction, and says this is his last birth.

Every Buddhist tradition tells some form of this scene, and in many temples an image of the newborn, one hand pointing up and one down, is bathed with sweet water on his birthday. Now the part that isn't legend.
A century or two after the Buddha's death, depending on whose dating you follow, the emperor Ashoka, who had become a Buddhist, came to Lumbini on pilgrimage and set up a stone pillar.
Its inscription says, in effect, that here the Buddha, the sage of the Sakyas, was born, and that because of this the village's taxes were lowered.
Lost for centuries, the pillar was found again in eighteen ninety-six. It still stands in southern Nepal, and pilgrims from all over the world walk there.
A real place, a real stone, and a story about arriving before you arrive: the most important birth in the tradition happened on the road, under a tree, on the way somewhere else.

how: Buddhists celebrate the Buddha's birth at Vesak, or in East Asia on a birthday festival in spring, often by pouring sweet water or tea over a small statue of the newborn Buddha; Lumbini, in Nepal, is one of the four great pilgrimage places.

games.q: you're Queen Maya, on the road to your parents' home. you pass a sal grove in full bloom. what do you do?
o: stop to walk in the garden.
games.why: she stops to walk in the garden, reaches for a sal branch, and gives birth there. the Buddha is born on the way, not at home.

practice: If you can, stand under a tree for a minute, in a yard, a street, a park; if you can't, picture one clearly, or look at a plant near you.

Feel the ground under your feet, look up into the branches, and notice that a tree is always in the middle of becoming something: budding, dropping, growing. Then close your eyes and let the breath be your garden.

wordCard.voice: Lumbini. The garden where the Buddha was born, on the road between two homes, marked by Ashoka's pillar in southern Nepal.

orig.note: The name of the garden where the Buddha was born, now in southern Nepal.

carryVoice: Your line: born on the way somewhere. Not at home, but on the road. See you tomorrow.
